title: Nesting and Indentation
summary: Shows how to nest a complete list inside a list item, why the parent li's closing tag must come after the nested list, and why consistent indentation is what makes nested HTML readable. The exercise builds a four-level nested list, and the walkthrough ends with VS Code auto-indentation and using indentation to find a missing closing tag.

concepts.heading: Nesting: elements inside elements
points: Nesting means placing one element inside another. You have already done it: every li sits inside a ul or ol, and the code shows that by indenting the li lines one level further than the list tags.
A list can also be nested inside another list. The inner ul/ol goes inside one of the outer list's li elements, never directly between li elements.
Rendered result: the inner list appears indented under the bullet (or number) of the li that contains it.
(Extra) Browsers change the default marker for deeper unordered levels: disc, then circle, then square.

concepts.heading: How to write a nested list
points: Find the li that should own the sub-list.

Write that li's own text first (e.g. B), press Enter, then write a complete new
    ...
or
    ...
with its own li items.
Only after the nested list's closing tag do you close the parent li. In a simple item the comes straight after the text; in an item that contains a sub-list the moves down to after the sub-list.
This is the key rule of the lesson: the closing tag of the outer element must come after everything nested inside it. Tags close in reverse order of opening.
You can repeat this to any depth, mixing ul and ol freely: an ordered list inside an unordered one, then an unordered one inside that, and so on.

concepts.heading: Why indentation matters
points: Indentation (leading spaces or tabs) has no effect on what the browser renders. It exists purely for the people reading the code.
With every nested level indented one step further, you can see at a glance which list belongs to which item. If everything is flush left, you have to read each tag name to work out the structure.

The more levels there are, the worse unindented code gets. The lecture shows the same three-list example (an outer ul, a ul under item B, and an ol under the second item of that ul) with and without indentation to make the point.
Write code with other readers in mind: teammates, reviewers, and you in a few months.

concepts.heading: VS Code helps: auto-indent and indent guides
points: Saving with Cmd+S (Mac) or Ctrl+S (Windows) re-indents the file automatically, because the formatter knows which elements belong inside which (e.g. li inside ul/ol). This works if format-on-save was enabled in the setup lessons.
So you do not have to indent perfectly by hand while typing, but you do need to understand what the indentation means.
VS Code draws thin vertical guide lines linking an opening tag to its matching closing tag; the children sit indented between them.
(Extra) You can also run Format Document on demand: Shift+Option+F on Mac, Shift+Alt+F on Windows.

concepts.heading: Using indentation to debug a missing closing tag
points: Most HTML elements come in pairs, so every opening tag should have a matching closing tag at the same indentation level.
Example from the walkthrough: delete the that should close the B1-B3 list. In the preview, item C suddenly shows up numbered as part of the ordered list instead of as a top-level bullet.

To diagnose it, follow the guide lines: the outer ul matches its closing tag, each li matches its closing tag, but the ol lines up with a closing instead of a closing . That mismatch points straight at the missing tag.
Finding and fixing mistakes like this is called debugging, which gets much more attention later in the course. Indentation is the first debugging tool.

concepts.heading: Exercise workflow tips
points: Download and extract the 'Nesting and Indentation' zip from the lecture Resources and open it in VS Code.
Keep goal.png open next to the Live Preview and compare after each step.
Build from the outside in: first the outer list, then the first sub-list, then the next level down, checking the preview each time.
The item names encode their position (B2a = item a of the list under B2), which tells you where each list belongs.

concepts.heading: (Extra) Vocabulary that the rest of the course relies on
points: An element directly inside another is its child; the wrapping element is its parent; elements with the same parent are siblings; anything inside at any depth is a descendant.
In the exercise, the ol (B1-B3) is a child of the li 'B' and a descendant of the outer ul.
These relationships drive CSS selectors and JavaScript DOM navigation later.

task.name: 3.2 Nesting and Indentation: four-level nested list
task.starting_point: index.html is the page to write the list into (the reference repo copy is already completed); goal.png shows the target nested list with items named A, B, C, B1, B2, B3, B2a, B2b, B2c, B2aa, B2ab, B31, B32.
task.goal: Recreate the goal's nested list structure exactly, using the right list type (ul for bullets, ol for numbers) at each level and correct nesting.
steps: Create the top-level ul with three li items: A, B, C. Check the preview.
Inside li 'B', after the text B, add an ol with three items: B1, B2, B3. Move B's closing to after this ol.
Inside li 'B2', after its text, add a ul with three items: B2a, B2b, B2c. Close B2's li after that ul.
Inside li 'B2a' (the first item, not the second), after its text, add a ul with B2aa and B2ab.
Inside li 'B3', after its text, add an ol with B31 and B32.
Save (Cmd/Ctrl+S) so VS Code re-indents everything, then compare the preview with goal.png level by level.
If something lands at the wrong level, follow the indent guides to find the opening tag whose closing partner is missing or misplaced.
task.expected_result: Bullets A, B, C at the top; under B a list numbered 1-3; under B2 three bullets; under B2a two further bullets; under B3 a list numbered 1-2. Preview identical to goal.png.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 03 - Intermediate HTML/03.02 - Nesting and Indentation/solution.html

pitfalls: Closing the parent straight after its text and then putting the sub-list after it. The sub-list then sits directly inside the outer ul/ol, which is invalid, and the structure no longer matches the goal.
Putting a nested list between two li elements instead of inside one.
Forgetting a closing or , which pulls later items (like C) into the wrong list.
Nesting B2aa/B2ab under B2b instead of B2a.
Using ul where the goal shows numbers (or ol where it shows bullets).
Assuming indentation changes the output. It does not; it only reveals the structure.
